prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current approaches for estimating the pose of articulated objects (objects with movable parts like drawers or laptop lids) predominantly rely on a multi-stage pipeline: first segmenting parts from a 3D point cloud, and then estimating the pose for each isolated segment. We identify two critical flaws in this paradigm. First, the "segment-then-pose" approach severs the global context; processing a part in isolation often leads to symmetry ambiguities (e.g., inability to distinguish the front from the back of a symmetric lid) and error accumulation. Second, existing methods rely heavily on geometric cues from depth sensors. This geometric reliance fails when dealing with small parts or noisy depth data, ignoring the dense, rich semantic information available in corresponding RGB images.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that articulated part perception should be solved as a unified, single-shot task rather than a cascaded series of sub-tasks. We hypothesize that fusing dense semantic features from modern RGB vision backbones with geometric point cloud data will allow a single network to simultaneously learn part semantics, instance differentiation, and canonical coordinates. By preserving the whole-object context during inference, we expect to resolve visual ambiguities that plague local-only methods and significantly improve the detection of small articulated components.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We aim to build a unified network (CAP-Net) that processes RGB-D data to output 6D pose and size for all articulated parts in an end-to-end manner.

**1. Multi-Modal Feature Fusion Strategy**
Instead of relying solely on point cloud geometry, we will extract dense semantic features from the RGB image using pre-trained vision encoders known for strong instance segmentation and high-resolution local features. These semantic embeddings will be projected and concatenated point-wise with geometric features extracted from the depth map (via a point-based backbone). This ensures every 3D point carries both geometric context and rich visual semantic data.

**2. Unified Multi-Task Prediction**
The fused features will be fed into three parallel decoding heads that operate simultaneously on the whole-object point cloud:
*   **Semantic Part Learner:** Classifies each point into specific part categories (e.g., handle, drawer, lid).
*   **Instance Centroid Offset Learner:** To handle multiple instances of the same part type (e.g., three identical handles), this module will predict a translation vector for every point, pointing towards the center of its respective part instance.
*   **Canonical Coordinate (NPCS) Learner:** This module will predict the Normalized Part Coordinate Space (NPCS) map for each point. This creates a dense correspondence between the observed object and a standardized canonical shape space.

**3. Instance Grouping and Pose Recovery**
We will employ a clustering algorithm on the predicted centroid offsets to group points into distinct instances. Once the instances are isolated, we will align the predicted NPCS maps with the observed camera-space point cloud. By solving for the transformation that aligns these two spaces, we can recover the final 6D pose and size for each articulated part without requiring explicit bounding box regression.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** A shift from multi-stage to single-shot articulated pose estimation, demonstrating that global context is essential for resolving pose ambiguity.
*   **Robustness:** A method that leverages RGB semantics to handle small parts and depth sensor noise effectively, outperforming geometry-only baselines.
*   **Sim-to-Real Transfer:** The introduction of a realistic rendering pipeline (photorealistic RGB + sensor-noise simulated depth) to allow models trained on synthetic data to generalize effectively to real-world robotic manipulation tasks.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Datasets
*   **Primary Dataset:** RGBD-Art (created for this study).
    *   **Source:** Based on objects from GAPartNet and PartNet-Mobility (URDF models).
    *   **Scale:** 1,045 object instances, 63,000 images, 408,000 part annotations.
    *   **Categories (9 Types):** Line fixed handle, round fixed handle, hinge handle, hinge lid, slider lid, slider button, slider drawer, hinge door, and hinge knob.
    *   **Generation Details:**
        *   **RGB:** Photorealistic rendering via ray-tracing with domain randomization (lighting, textures, materials).
        *   **Depth:** Simulated active stereo depth camera noise (patterned after RealSense D415) rather than idealized depth.
        *   **Views:** 60 random camera views per background (2 backgrounds per instance).
*   **Real-World Data:** Images captured using a RealSense D435 camera for robotic experiments.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **3D Semantic Instance Segmentation:**
    *   **AP50:** Average Precision at 50% IoU threshold.
    *   **AP:** Average Precision across IoU thresholds from 50% to 95% (intervals of 5%).
*   **Pose & Size Estimation:**
    *   **$R_e$:** Average rotation error (degrees).
    *   **$T_e$:** Average translation error (cm).
    *   **$S_e$:** Average scale/size error (cm).
    *   **$d_e$:** Translation error along the interaction axis (cm).
    *   **3D mIoU:** 3D Intersection over Union.
    *   **$A_5$:** Accuracy percentage for thresholds of 5° and 5 cm.
    *   **$A_{10}$:** Accuracy percentage for thresholds of 10° and 10 cm.

### Baselines Compared
*   **PointGroup:** Adapted for part-based 3D semantic instance segmentation and pose estimation.
*   **SoftGroup:** Adapted for part-based tasks.
*   **AutoGPart:** Adapted for part-based tasks.
*   **GAPartNet:** The state-of-the-art method (two-stage approach).

### Implementation Details
*   **Hardware:** 4 NVIDIA L20 GPUs, Intel i9-13900K CPU.
*   **Training Configuration:**
    *   **Epochs:** 100.
    *   **Batch Size:** 4.
    *   **Optimizer:** Initial learning rate 0.001 with a warm-up scheduler.
*   **Input Specifications:**
    *   **Images:** Cropped and resized to 640 x 640 resolution.
    *   **Point Clouds:** Randomly sampled to 24,576 points.
*   **Multi-task Loss Weights:**
    *   Semantic segmentation ($\lambda_1$): 17.5
    *   Instance offset learning ($\lambda_2$): 125
    *   NPCS mapping ($\lambda_3$): 0.15
*   **Feature Extractors:** Pretrained SAM2 encoder (dense features) and FeatUp encoder (high-resolution, SE(3)-consistent features).
*   **Backbone:** PointNet++.

---

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Global Context vs. Local Segments:**
    *   Observation: Approaches that first segment parts and then estimate pose (like GAPartNet) suffer from visual ambiguity. For example, when viewing only the top part of a laptop (without the base), it is difficult to distinguish the front from the back, leading to 180-degree rotation errors.
    *   Observation: By processing the complete object (global context), our method resolves ambiguities such as mirrored symmetries in hinged lids or doors, which local-input methods often misclassify.
*   **Impact of RGB Features:**
    *   Observation: Purely geometric (point-cloud based) baselines struggled to distinguish small components, such as buttons on a remote control, due to depth noise.
    *   Observation: The integration of dense RGB semantic features allowed for the successful segmentation and identification of small parts that were otherwise indistinguishable in the depth data.
*   **Sim-to-Real Transfer:**
    *   Observation: The model trained on the proposed RGBD-Art dataset (with photorealistic RGB and simulated depth noise) generalized effectively to real-world data captured by a consumer-grade RealSense camera.
    *   Observation: Baselines trained on synthetic data without realistic depth noise patterns showed a significant drop in accuracy when applied to real-world noisy depth data.
*   **Robotic Interaction:**
    *   Observation: In physical experiments, the generated poses were accurate enough to guide a robotic arm to successfully manipulate unseen articulated objects (pulling drawers, lifting lids, rotating handles).
    *   Observation: The baseline (GAPartNet) often failed in these tasks due to pose estimation errors, specifically incorrect orientation predictions.

  - Caption: Figure 4. Architecture overview. CAP-Net uses pretrained vision backbones, SAM2 [28] and FeatUp [9], to extract dense semantic features, which are then fused with the point cloud in a point-wise manner. The enriched point cloud features are passed into PointNet++ [27] for further processing. These features are then used by three parallel modules to predict semantic labels, centroid offsets, and NPCS maps. A clustering algorithm groups points with the same semantic label based on centroid distances to isolate each possible part. Finally, an alignment algorithm matches the predicted NPCS map with the real point cloud to estimate each part’s pose and size.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

```

   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}

  \end{subfigure}

    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Robotic manipulation of articulated objects (e.g., opening drawers, turning handles) requires precise estimation of the 6D pose and size of individual moving parts. Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on "first-segment-then-pose" pipelines. These methods first segment parts from a 3D point cloud and subsequently estimate the Normalized Part Coordinate Space (NPCS) for each segment. This cascaded approach suffers from two critical failures:
1.  **Error Accumulation:** Segmentation errors in the first stage propagate to the pose estimation stage, leading to suboptimal accuracy.
2.  **Loss of Global Context:** By processing segmented parts in isolation, the network loses global context, resulting in visual ambiguities (e.g., inability to distinguish the front from the back of a symmetrical object like a laptop lid).
Furthermore, existing methods rely heavily on geometric cues from depth sensors, which often lack sufficient resolution for small parts (buttons, thin handles) and ignore dense semantic cues available in RGB images. Finally, there is a significant sim-to-real gap; existing synthetic datasets lack photorealistic RGB rendering and realistic depth sensor noise models.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **CAP-Net** (Categorical Articulated Parts Network), a unified, single-stage architecture that estimates 6D pose and size for articulated parts directly from a single RGB-D image.

Our core hypothesis is that fusing dense, high-resolution semantic features from pre-trained vision backbones (specifically SAM2 and FeatUp) with geometric point cloud features will enable robust part identification and pose estimation in an end-to-end manner. By simultaneously predicting point-wise semantic labels, centroid offsets, and NPCS maps within a unified network, we can utilize global object context to resolve ambiguities and improve performance on small parts. Additionally, we hypothesize that training on a newly generated dataset featuring ray-traced RGB and simulated sensor noise will effectively bridge the sim-to-real domain gap.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a single-shot framework that processes an input RGB-D image patch to recover the 6-DoF pose and 3D size of all articulated parts.

### 1. Data Generation (RGBD-Art Dataset)
To support this architecture, we will generate a large-scale synthetic dataset.
*   **RGB Generation:** We will employ ray-tracing to generate photorealistic images with domain randomization (lighting, textures, materials).
*   **Depth Simulation:** We will simulate active stereo depth camera noise (patterned after RealSense D415) rather than using ideal depth maps, ensuring the model learns to handle real-world geometric noise.
*   **Annotations:** Canonical orientation and NPCS normalization for 9 categories of articulated parts.

### 2. Task Formulation
Given an RGB-D image patch $(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{D})$, where $\mathcal{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ is the RGB image and $\mathcal{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$ is the depth map, we aim to estimate three outputs for each point $i$ in the back-projected point cloud $\mathcal{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$:
1.  Semantic class label $c_i$.
2.  Normalized Part Coordinate Space (NPCS) map $m_i$.
3.  Centroid offset $o_i$ (vector to the instance center).

The final goal is to compute pose parameters $\{\mathbf{R}_k, \mathbf{t}_k, \mathbf{s}_k\}$ for the $k$-th part instance, where $\mathbf{R}_k \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$, $\mathbf{t}_k \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{s}_k \in \mathbb{R}^3$.

### 3. Feature Extraction and Fusion Architecture
We will construct a dual-branch feature extraction pipeline:
1.  **Semantic Branch:** We will utilize the pre-trained **SAM2** encoder to extract features of size $H \times W \times 96$ and the **FeatUp** encoder to extract high-resolution, SE(3)-consistent features of size $H \times W \times 384$. These will be concatenated to form a dense semantic embedding of dimension 480 per pixel.
2.  **Geometric Branch & Fusion:** We will back-project the depth map to a 3D point cloud $\mathcal{P}$. We will concatenate the 480-dimensional RGB feature vector to its corresponding 3D point in a point-wise manner.
3.  **Backbone:** The fused RGB-D point cloud will be processed by a **PointNet++** backbone to extract dense features for downstream decoding.

### 4. Multi-Task Learning Modules
The network will branch into three parallel decoders ($\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{sem}}$, $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{inst}}$, $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{npcs}}$), trained jointly.

#### A. Semantic Part Learning ($\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{sem}}$)
This module predicts the semantic class of each point. We will formulate this as a classification task supervised by Focal Loss:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} FL(\hat{c}_i, c_i) $$
where $N$ is the number of points, $\hat{c}_i$ is the predicted label, and $c_i$ is the ground-truth class label.

#### B. Centroid Offset Learning ($\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{inst}}$)
To distinguish between multiple instances of the same part class, we will predict a translation offset $\Delta o_i$ from each point $p_i$ to its instance center. This clusters points spatially. The loss is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inst}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} ||\Delta o_i - \Delta \hat{o}_i|| \cdot \mathbb{I}(p_i \in S_k) $$
where $\Delta \hat{o}_i$ is the predicted offset, $\Delta o_i$ is the ground truth, and $\mathbb{I}(p_i \in S_k)$ is an indicator function that is 1 if point $p_i$ belongs to instance $S_k$.

#### C. NPCS Learning ($\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{npcs}}$)
We will learn the mapping from the observed point cloud $\mathcal{P}$ to the canonical space $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{C}}$. We will discretize the NPCS coordinates into 32 bins per axis and treat this as a classification problem to reduce the solution space. The supervision uses Softmax Cross-Entropy ($SCE$):
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{npcs}} = \frac{1}{3N} \sum_{n=1}^{3} \sum_{i=1}^{N} SCE(\hat{m}_i^n, m_i^n) $$
where $\hat{m}_i^n$ and $m_i^n$ are the predicted and ground truth discrete NPCS labels for the $n$-th axis (x, y, z).

#### D. Total Loss
The network will be optimized end-to-end using a weighted sum of the three losses:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}} + \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inst}} + \lambda_3 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{npcs}} $$

### 5. Post-Processing and Pose Recovery
During inference, we will execute the following steps:
1.  **Clustering:** Filter points by predicted semantic label. Apply **DBSCAN** on the predicted instance centers ($p_i + \Delta \hat{o}_i$) to group points into distinct instances $S_k$.
2.  **Alignment:** For each instance $S_k$, we will use the **Umeyama algorithm** (with RANSAC for outlier removal) to align the predicted canonical points (from NPCS map) with the observed 3D points. This alignment yields the rotation $\mathbf{R}_k$, translation $\mathbf{t}_k$, and scale $\mathbf{s}_k$.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Architecture:** We will provide the first RGB-D method to estimate semantic labels, instance centers, and NPCS representations in a single-shot, end-to-end process, eliminating the error accumulation inherent in multi-stage pipelines.
2.  **Enhanced Small-Part Perception:** By integrating dense semantic features from SAM2/FeatUp, we expect to significantly improve the detection and pose estimation of small articulated parts (e.g., knobs, buttons) that are often invisible to geometry-only methods.
3.  **Sim-to-Real Transfer:** Through the creation of the RGBD-Art dataset with physically grounded sensor noise and photorealism, we aim to enable direct transfer of the trained model to real-world robotic manipulation tasks using low-cost sensors (e.g., RealSense) without fine-tuning.

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists.
